w: Built in 1180 as the seat of the Counts of Flanders, the Gravensteen kept that job only until 1353, after which it did time as a courthouse, a prison, a mint and even a cotton mill before Ghent restored it around 1900. Moat, battlements and all, it's the city's most photographed medieval leftover.
s: A count's castle that became a prison, then a cotton mill
_facts: medieval water castle, current structure dates from 1180
residence of the Counts of Flanders until 1353
later repurposed as a court, prison, mint and cotton mill
restored 1893-1903; now a museum and major city landmark

w: Ghent's Gothic cathedral rises 89 metres over the city and holds, inside one modest chapel, one of the most famous paintings ever made: the Ghent Altarpiece, also known as the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb. Seat of the Diocese of Ghent, and worth the visit for that single artwork alone.
s: Home to one of the world's most famous altarpieces
_facts: 89m-tall Gothic Roman Catholic cathedral, seat of the Diocese of Ghent
named for Saint Bavo of Ghent
houses the Ghent Altarpiece (Adoration of the Mystic Lamb)

w: Built as the cultural headquarters of Ghent's labour movement, Vooruit once packed a ballroom, a cinema and a theatre under one roof for workers who built their own art centre rather than wait for one. It still hosts concerts and cultural events today, decades removed from its socialist origins.
s: The labour movement's own ballroom and cinema
_facts: historic complex, originally the festival and art centre of the Ghent labour movement
housed a ballroom, cinema and theatre
now mainly used for concerts and cultural events

w: Begun in the 1200s in the local Scheldt Gothic style, blue-gray stone from Tournai, one broad tower over the crossing, St. Nicholas served the guilds working the old Korenmarkt trade centre next door, each adding its own chapel over the centuries. Before Ghent's Belfry existed, this tower carried the town bells.
s: The tower that rang Ghent's bells before the Belfry existed
_facts: 13th-century Roman Catholic church, one of the oldest landmarks in Ghent
built in the local Scheldt Gothic style, using blue-gray Tournai stone
guilds working the nearby Korenmarkt added their own chapels in the 14th-15th centuries
its tower carried the town bells before the neighbouring Belfry was built

w: Designed around 1900 by Ghent's own city architect and reopened in 2007 after a four-year restoration, the MSK holds some 9,000 works spanning the Middle Ages to the 20th century, with roughly 600 on permanent view, a founding partner of the Flemish Art Collection alongside Bruges' Groeninge Museum.
s: 9,000 artworks in a restored Belle Epoque building
_facts: art museum beside Citadelpark; collection of some 9,000 artworks, Middle Ages to 20th century
around 600 works on permanent display
building designed c.1900 by city architect Charles van Rysselberghe
reopened 2007 after a four-year restoration; part of the Flemish Art Collection with the Groeninge Museum, Bruges

w: Once the working quay of Ghent's medieval port, the Graslei is now better known for its row of gabled guildhalls and the café terraces packed along the water. Its twin quay, Korenlei, faces it across the Leie: together they're the view every postcard of Ghent is built around.
s: Ghent's medieval waterfront, now lined with café terraces
_facts: quay on the right bank of the Leie in the historic centre, part of the medieval port
opposite quay is Korenlei
now a cultural and touristic hotspot with a row of historical buildings
the site is a protected cityscape

w: Ghent dropped this vast freestanding canopy right into the square framed by the Belfry, the Renaissance town hall and St. Nicholas' Church, and locals were not shy about hating it when it went up in 2012. Modern steel and timber sitting squarely inside seven centuries of stone, still dividing opinion.
s: A giant modern roof dropped between three medieval landmarks
_facts: large stand-alone canopy in the inner city, part of a public-space redevelopment project
sits on the square between the Belfry, the Renaissance Town Hall and St Nicholas' Church
criticised on construction in 2012 for its size, height and modern materials amid historic surroundings

w: Tucked into southern Ghent between two long-vanished city gates, the Hooipoort and the Vijfwindgatenpoort, this small beguinage takes its name from the 'Groene Hooie' meadow it once stood on. One of a handful of beguinages that still mark the city's map, easy to walk past and easy to miss.
s: A tiny beguinage named after a vanished city gate
_facts: small beguinage in southern Ghent
built on the 'Groene Hooie', between the old Hooipoort and Vijfwindgatenpoort gates
name derives from that site

w: STAM traces its roots to 1833, but its current home is the Bijloke, a medieval monastery repurposed as the city's own history museum since 2010. Chronological rooms walk visitors from Ghent's past to its present and future, with a section devoted to the Ghent Altarpiece. Flemish Museum Prize winner, 2012.
s: Ghent's own history, told inside a medieval abbey
_facts: city history museum, opened 9 October 2010; roots trace to an 1833 antiquities museum
housed in the Bijloke abbey and monastery buildings
chronological rooms cover the city's past, present and future, with a section on the Ghent Altarpiece
won the 2012 Flemish Museum Prize

w: A Lourdes grotto built in a marquise's garden in 1873 drew crowds after a reported miracle cure two years later, a man's compound fracture said to have healed on the spot. The neo-Gothic basilica raised for the pilgrims became Flanders' top Marian shrine, its 49-bell carillon still hanging in the tower.
s: A grotto miracle that grew into a top pilgrimage site
_facts: neogothic Basilica of Our Lady of Lourdes, most important centre of Marian pilgrimage in Flanders
grotto built 1873 by the Marquise of Courtebourne-de Nedonchel; claimed miraculous healing of Pieter De Rudder in 1875
basilica completed 1876, consecrated 1877, entrusted to the Jesuits
carillon of 49 bells cast in the 1950s; keyboard removed during 1970s renovation, never replaced

w: Ghent's Campo Santo has been declared a historical monument in its own right, its rows of graves and sculpture treated as heritage rather than just a working cemetery. Tucked into Sint-Amandsberg, it's a quiet counterpart to the busier landmarks nearer the centre.
_facts: Roman Catholic public burial ground in Sint-Amandsberg
declared a historical monument by the government

w: Known simply as the Holy Corner, this is one of three beguinages that still dot Ghent's map, its sister foundation sits out in Sint-Amandsberg, both named for Elizabeth of Hungary. A third, Our-Lady Ter Hooyen, holds the south side of the city. Together they trace a quieter, older Ghent between the modern streets.
s: One of three beguinages still marking Ghent's map
_facts: also known as the Great or Old St. Elizabeth Beguinage
one of three beguinages in Ghent, alongside the New St. Elizabeth Beguinage (Sint-Amandsberg) and Our-Lady Ter Hooyen
both St. Elizabeth beguinages named after Elizabeth of Hungary

w: Named for St. Peter's Abbey along its eastern flank, this is Ghent's largest public square, and its calendar is busiest every March, when the Mid-Lent Fair takes over. The square and its surrounding buildings are protected as a cityscape, so the abbey's old backdrop isn't going anywhere.
s: Ghent's biggest square, home to a March fair for generations
_facts: Sint-Pietersplein, Ghent's largest public square, south of the historic centre
named after St Peter's Abbey on its east side
regular venue for cultural and sporting events, including the annual Mid-Lent Fair in March
the square and surrounding buildings are a protected cityscape
